questions.q: Define 'family of orientation' and 'family of procreation' and give one example of how a person belongs to both simultaneously.
questions.a: Family of orientation is the family into which a person is born and raised (parents, siblings); family of procreation is the family formed through marriage (spouse, children). Example: A married woman belongs to her natal family (orientation) and her marital family (procreation) simultaneously. A wrong answer that defines both as "the family you live with" reveals confusion between residence and kinship ties — the student fails to distinguish structural position from household composition.

questions.q: A student claims: "The functionalist view says nuclear families are better for industrial society because women are naturally nurturing and men are naturally breadwinners." Identify two errors in this statement using sociological terminology.
questions.a: Error 1: The functionalist argument (Parsons/Giddens) is about role specialization (instrumental vs affective) as a structural requirement of industrial economy, not biological determinism — "naturally" confuses social role with biological essence. Error 2: The NCERT text explicitly states this vision is "questionable not just because it is gender unjust but because empirical studies... show that it is untrue" (garment export industry employs women). A wrong answer focusing only on "gender unjust" misses the empirical falsification; a wrong answer citing "modern families are different" misses the structural argument about role specialization.

questions.q: In a village in Haryana, 65-year-old Ram Singh lives with his wife, their married son, daughter-in-law, and two grandchildren. His married daughter visits during festivals. Using A.M. Shah's framework, explain why this household is classified as joint despite the daughter's non-residence, and what demographic trend makes such households more common.
questions.a: Classification: Joint family because it contains two generations of married brothers (or father-son) sharing residence and kitchen — the defining criterion is co-residence of multiple married couples in the same household, not inclusion of all kin. Demographic trend: Rising life expectancy (from 32.5 to 55.4 years for men, 1941-50 to 1981-85) increased the proportion of aged (60+) in population; most elderly live in joint households with adult children. A wrong answer saying "because the daughter visits" confuses visiting kin with resident members; a wrong answer citing "tradition" misses the demographic mechanism Shah identifies.

questions.q: Compare the Kolam female-headed household (accepted norm) with the migrant female-headed household (husband stops sending remittances). Analyze how the same structural form (female-headed) emerges from different causal mechanisms — one cultural, one economic — and what this implies for the "patriarchy is universal" claim.
questions.a: Kolam: Female headship is a culturally institutionalized norm (matrilineal/matrilocal context) where women's authority is legitimate and permanent. Migrant: Female headship is a contingent, often temporary adaptation to male migration and remittance failure — women assume provider role out of necessity, not cultural prescription. Implication: Patriarchy is not universal in form or rigidity; female-headed households can be normative (Kolam) or reactive (migrant), proving that gender authority structures vary by kinship system and political economy. A wrong answer treating both as "women forced to take charge" erases the cultural legitimacy in Kolam society and misreads structural diversity as uniform oppression.

questions.q: Critique the modernization theory prediction that "industrialization inevitably leads to nuclear family dominance" using three pieces of empirical evidence from the Indian context provided in the NCERT text.
questions.a: Evidence 1: A.M. Shah documents joint family increase in post-independence India (1941-50 to 1981-85) alongside industrialization, driven by rising life expectancy — contradicting unilinear nuclearization. Evidence 2: Singh (1993) shows families "need not become nuclear in an industrial pattern of economy" — Indian industrial workers maintain joint/extended ties for mutual aid. Evidence 3: German unification case — withdrawal of state welfare caused marriage decline, proving family form responds to state policy, not just industrial logic. A critique using only "joint families still exist" without citing the demographic mechanism (Shah) or the policy mechanism (German case) fails to engage the theoretical claim at the structural level.

questions.q: Construct a kinship diagram for a matrilocal, matrilineal society where the maternal uncle holds authority (avunculate). Show three generations, label all consanguineous and affinal ties, and indicate residence, descent, and authority flows with arrows. Write a 3-sentence sociological interpretation of how this structure challenges the "patriarchal nuclear family as universal" assumption.
questions.a: [Diagram description: Generation 1: Maternal grandmother (head) ↔ maternal grandfather (affine). Generation 2: Mother (resident) — Father (affine, non-resident visitor) — Maternal uncle (resident, authority holder). Generation 3: Ego (child) — Siblings — Maternal uncle's children (consanguineous). Arrows: Descent ↓ through women; Residence → matrilocal (husband visits); Authority → maternal uncle.] Interpretation: This structure separates biological fatherhood from social fathering (uncle), residence from descent, and authority from conjugal unit — demonstrating that child-rearing, inheritance, and power can be organized without a co-resident husband-father. A poor diagram showing father as resident head or missing the uncle's authority reveals inability to decenter the patriarchal nuclear model.
